content: The common cold typically presents with symptoms such as a runny nose, nasal congestion, and sneezing. Additional symptoms may include a sore throat, cough, headache, or other discomforts. Symptoms of the Common Cold Symptoms of a cold usually appear within 2 to 3 days after exposure to the virus, though it can take up to a week. The symptoms primarily affect the nasal passages. The most common symptoms include: Nasal congestion Runny nose Scratchy throat Sneezing Adults and older children with colds generally experience either no fever or a low-grade fever. However, younger children often develop a fever ranging from 100°F to 102°F. Depending on the specific virus causing the cold, additional symptoms may include: Cough Decreased appetite Headache Muscle aches Postnasal drip Sore throat Causes of the Common Cold The term common cold is fitting, as there are over one billion cases annually in the United States. Both adults and children are more likely to experience colds than any other illness. Colds are a leading cause of school absences for children and work absences for parents. Parents often contract colds from their children, who typically experience up to eight colds per year, often transmitted by other children. Colds spread rapidly in environments like schools and daycare centers. While colds can occur year-round, they are most prevalent during the winter or rainy seasons. The cold virus spreads through tiny airborne droplets released when an infected person sneezes, coughs, or blows their nose. You can catch a cold if: An infected person sneezes, coughs, or blows their nose near you. You touch your nose, eyes, or mouth after coming into contact with a contaminated surface, such as a toy or doorknob. The disease is most contagious during the first 2 to 3 days of symptoms but becomes less contagious after the first week. Diagnosis The diagnosis of a common cold is primarily based on symptoms, which may include weakness, runny nose, sneezing, or coughing. There are no specific laboratory, imaging, or other diagnostic tests required to confirm a common cold. However, certain symptoms, such as a high fever, severe fatigue, or a productive cough, may suggest a more serious condition and warrant further investigation. Treatment Options Primary Treatment Rest and Hydration: Ensure adequate rest and drink plenty of fluids. Cold Medications: Over-the-counter cold and cough medications may alleviate symptoms in adults and older children. While these medications do not shorten the duration of the cold, they can provide symptomatic relief. Children Under 6: Over-the-counter cold and cough medications are not recommended for children under the age of 6. Consult a doctor before giving any medication to children, even if labeled for pediatric use, as these medications may not be effective and could cause serious side effects. Antibiotics Antibiotics should not be used to treat the common cold, as they are ineffective against viral infections and may worsen the situation. Thick yellow or green nasal discharge is a normal part of a cold and does not require antibiotics unless symptoms persist beyond 10 to 14 days, in which case a doctor may prescribe antibiotics. Other Medications Newer antiviral drugs designed to relieve flu symptoms do not reduce cold symptoms. Alternative Treatments Chicken Soup: This traditional remedy may help due to its warmth, fluid content, and saltiness, which can aid in fighting the infection. Vitamin C: While regular intake of vitamin C does not prevent colds in most adults, it may slightly shorten the duration and severity of symptoms. However, taking vitamin C after the onset of symptoms does not appear to be beneficial. Zinc: Zinc supplements taken for at least 5 days may reduce the risk of catching a cold. Taking zinc within 24 hours of symptom onset may lessen the severity and duration of symptoms. Echinacea: This herb has been promoted as a natural remedy for preventing colds and flu or reducing symptom severity. However, high-quality studies have not demonstrated its effectiveness in preventing or treating colds. Alternative treatments are generally safe for most people but may cause side effects or allergic reactions. For example, some individuals are allergic to echinacea. Herbs and supplements may also interact with other medications. Consult your doctor before trying alternative treatments. When to Seek Medical Care Attempt to manage your cold at home initially. Contact your doctor if: You experience difficulty breathing. Your symptoms worsen or do not improve after 7 to 10 days. Prognosis During a cold, nasal discharge may thicken and turn yellow or green within a few days. This is normal and does not require antibiotics. Most cold symptoms resolve within a week. If symptoms persist beyond 7 days, consult your doctor to rule out conditions such as sinus infections, allergies, or other medical issues. Possible Complications The common cold is the most frequent trigger of asthma symptoms in children with asthma. It may also lead to: Bronchitis Ear infections Pneumonia Sinusitis Prevention To reduce the risk of catching a cold: 1. Handwashing: Wash hands frequently, especially after nose-wiping, diaper changes, using the bathroom, and before eating or preparing food. 2. Disinfection: Clean commonly touched surfaces, such as sink handles, doorknobs, and sleeping mats, with an EPA-approved disinfectant. 3. Smaller Daycare Classes: Enroll children in daycare settings with fewer than seven children to reduce germ spread. 4. Hand Sanitizers: Use alcohol-based hand sanitizers to kill germs. These are antiseptic, not antibiotic, and do not contribute to resistance. 5. Paper Towels: Use disposable paper towels instead of shared cloth towels. To strengthen your immune system: Avoid secondhand smoke, which contributes to numerous health problems, including colds. Avoid unnecessary antibiotics to prevent antibiotic resistance. Breastfeed infants, as breast milk protects against respiratory infections and reduces the risk of ear infections. Stay hydrated by drinking water. Consume yogurt with active cultures, which may help prevent colds. Get sufficient sleep, as sleep deprivation increases susceptibility to illness.
